questions.stem: In What Is to Be Done? (1902), Lenin argued that revolution in Russia required:
options: a small, disciplined party of professional revolutionaries to lead the workers
a broad mass party open to anyone who supported the workers' cause
a long period of capitalist democracy before any socialist party could be formed at all
an alliance with the liberal Kadets to win a majority in the Duma
questions.explanation: Lenin's idea of a vanguard party of professional revolutionaries was the core of Bolshevism and caused the 1903 split with the Mensheviks, who wanted a broader party. Waiting for a long bourgeois-democratic stage was closer to the Menshevik view.

questions.stem: The October 1917 seizure of power is often called a coup rather than a popular revolution because:
options: the Provisional Government handed power to the Bolsheviks voluntarily in a signed agreement
it was carried out by the Tsar's former officers, who then invited Lenin to govern
armed units directed by the Military Revolutionary Committee took key points in Petrograd in a planned operation
the Bolsheviks had already won a clear majority of seats in the elected Constituent Assembly
questions.explanation: Red Guards and soldiers organised by the Petrograd Soviet's Military Revolutionary Committee, with Trotsky prominent, seized bridges, stations and the Winter Palace in a planned action involving relatively few people. The Constituent Assembly elections came after October, and the Bolsheviks did not win them.

questions.stem: Which slogan best summarises the Bolshevik program that won support in Petrograd between April and October 1917?
options: 'Defend the revolution and fight the war on to final victory'
'Socialism in one country' and 'liquidate the kulaks'
'Enrich yourselves' and 'the commanding heights'
'Peace, Land and Bread' and 'All power to the soviets'
questions.explanation: Lenin's April Theses demanded an end to the war, land for the peasants and power to the soviets, and these slogans drew workers and soldiers to the Bolsheviks. 'Revolutionary defencism' was the policy of the Provisional Government and moderate socialists, and the other slogans belong to the 1920s.

questions.stem: Which policy did the Bolsheviks use during the Civil War to feed the Red Army and the cities?
options: War Communism, including forced requisitioning of grain
the New Economic Policy, including a tax in kind
the First Five-Year Plan, including targets for heavy industry
collectivisation, including the creation of kolkhozes
questions.explanation: War Communism (1918-1921) nationalised industry, banned private trade and seized grain from peasants. The NEP replaced it in 1921, and the Five-Year Plans and collectivisation came under Stalin from 1928-29.

questions.stem: Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy in March 1921 mainly because:
options: the Comintern ordered the Soviet state to copy the economic policies of Germany
industrial output had risen so fast that rationing was no longer needed at all
peasant revolts, famine and the Kronstadt rising showed War Communism had to end
the Whites had won the Civil War and forced the Bolsheviks to accept a capitalist economy
questions.explanation: By 1921 the economy had collapsed, peasants were in revolt in places such as Tambov, and the Kronstadt sailors rebelled. Lenin restored private trade and replaced requisitioning with a tax in kind to win back the peasants. The Reds, not the Whites, won the Civil War.

questions.stem: The NEP is important background to Stalin's rise because:
options: it was designed by Trotsky, so its success made him the obvious successor to Lenin
it was abolished by Lenin before his death, leaving no economic debate for the 1920s
it had the full support of every party leader, so the power struggle was purely a personal one
party members divided over whether to keep it, and Stalin used the dispute to defeat rivals
questions.explanation: The Left (Trotsky, later Zinoviev and Kamenev) wanted to end the NEP and industrialise fast, while the Right (Bukharin) wanted to keep it. Stalin sided with the Right to defeat the Left, then adopted rapid industrialisation to defeat the Right. Lenin introduced the NEP and it lasted until about 1928.

questions.stem: After Lenin's death in January 1924, Stalin first allied with which two leaders against Trotsky?
options: Bukharin and Rykov
Molotov and Voroshilov
Tomsky and Yagoda
Zinoviev and Kamenev
questions.explanation: Stalin, Zinoviev and Kamenev formed a triumvirate against Trotsky in 1923-1925. Stalin later allied with Bukharin, Rykov and Tomsky on the Right against the United Opposition of Trotsky, Zinoviev and Kamenev.

questions.stem: Trotsky's theory of 'permanent revolution' differed from Stalin's 'Socialism in One Country' because Trotsky:
options: believed the Soviet Union should abandon communism entirely and return to a market economy
believed peasants, not workers, should be the main force in the Soviet revolution
believed the Soviet Union should avoid any contact with foreign communist parties
believed the Soviet revolution could survive only if revolution spread to other countries
questions.explanation: Trotsky argued that backward Russia needed revolutions in advanced countries to build socialism. Stalin's slogan of 1924 claimed socialism could be built in the USSR alone, which appealed to patriotic party members tired of waiting for world revolution.

questions.stem: How did the 'Lenin Enrolment' of 1924 help Stalin?
options: it gave the secret police the power to choose the delegates to every party congress
it brought in many new, inexperienced members who owed their place to the party apparatus Stalin ran
it made Stalin the only party leader allowed to speak to new members at party congresses
it expelled all Old Bolsheviks who had joined the party before the 1917 revolution
questions.explanation: Hundreds of thousands of workers joined the party after Lenin's death. As General Secretary, Stalin's Secretariat handled membership and appointments, and the new members tended to be loyal to the apparatus rather than to the old intellectual leaders such as Trotsky.

questions.stem: Lenin's 'Testament' did not harm Stalin as much as it might have because:
options: it was found only in 1956, long after Stalin had already died in office
Stalin had it read aloud to every party branch, so it lost its shock value
the party leadership agreed in 1924 not to publish it to the party as a whole
Lenin had praised Stalin in it as his chosen successor and most able colleague
questions.explanation: Lenin had recommended removing Stalin as General Secretary, but in May 1924 the Central Committee agreed to read it only to congress delegates and not publish it, with Zinoviev and Kamenev defending Stalin. Lenin criticised Stalin in it, and Khrushchev quoted it openly in 1956.

questions.stem: By the end of 1929, which leader of the 'Right' had been removed from the Politburo?
options: Sergei Kirov
Nikolai Bukharin
Leon Trotsky
Lev Kamenev
questions.explanation: Bukharin, with Rykov and Tomsky, opposed the end of the NEP and forced collectivisation, and was removed from the Politburo in November 1929. Trotsky and Kamenev belonged to the Left, and Kirov was a Stalin loyalist.

questions.stem: A historian argues that Stalin rose to power mainly through control of the party machine rather than through ideas. Which evidence best supports this?
options: As General Secretary he appointed regional secretaries who chose congress delegates loyal to him
He wrote the most influential works of Marxist theory of any party leader of the 1920s
He won a series of open elections against Trotsky held among all Soviet citizens
He commanded the Red Army during the Civil War, which made soldiers loyal to him
questions.explanation: Appointing secretaries meant that the delegates who voted at congresses were often Stalin's men, so his opponents were outvoted. Stalin was not a leading theorist, there were no such open elections, and it was Trotsky who built and led the Red Army.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why Trotsky, the best-known Bolshevik after Lenin, lost the power struggle?
options: He had opposed the October seizure of power and was blamed for the defeat in the Civil War
He supported the NEP so strongly that the Left of the party turned against him in 1924
He refused to take any government post after 1917 and so had no base of support at all
Other leaders feared him as a potential Napoleon, and he was a poor builder of alliances inside the party
questions.explanation: Trotsky's command of the Red Army made colleagues fear a Bonapartist takeover, and his arrogance and late joining of the Bolsheviks (1917) counted against him. He played a central part in October and led the Reds to victory, and he was a critic of the NEP.

questions.stem: The model of totalitarianism set out by Carl Friedrich and Zbigniew Brzezinski in 1956 included:
options: free elections, an independent judiciary, and a free market economy with private ownership
rule by a hereditary monarch supported by the church and the landed nobility
a weak central government that left local regions to run their own affairs
an official ideology, a single mass party, terror, and control of the media and economy
questions.explanation: Their 'six-point syndrome' was an ideology, a single party, a terroristic police, a monopoly of communications, a monopoly of weapons and a centrally directed economy. Historians have applied it to Stalin's USSR and Nazi Germany.

questions.stem: Revisionist historians such as J. Arch Getty challenged the totalitarian model of Stalinism mainly by arguing that:
options: the regime was often chaotic, and pressures from local officials and below shaped events such as the Terror
Stalin had no real power at all and was only a figurehead for the secret police chiefs
the Soviet state under Stalin was a genuine democracy in which workers chose the policies
the Terror never happened, and the reports of mass arrests were Western propaganda
questions.explanation: Revisionists argued that the centre's control was weaker and more improvised than the totalitarian model suggested, and that rivalries and local initiatives drove much of the repression. They did not deny the Terror or claim Stalin was powerless; Robert Conquest represents the contrasting totalitarian view.

questions.stem: The 'cult of personality' around Stalin in the 1930s presented him mainly as:
options: a humble official who carried out the decisions of the Central Committee
a military hero whose battlefield victories had won the Civil War alone
a modest worker who refused all public honours and portraits of himself
the wise leader, Lenin's true heir and the father of the Soviet peoples
questions.explanation: Posters, statues, renamed cities and rewritten history presented Stalin as the 'Lenin of today', a genius and a father figure. The cult took off around his fiftieth birthday in December 1929 and helped legitimise his personal rule.

questions.stem: The assassination of which Leningrad party leader in December 1934 was used to justify a wave of repression?
options: Felix Dzerzhinsky
Sergei Kirov
Grigory Zinoviev
Mikhail Tukhachevsky
questions.explanation: Kirov's murder on 1 December 1934 led to an emergency decree that sped up trials of 'terrorists' and to the arrest of many former oppositionists. Zinoviev was arrested after it, Tukhachevsky was shot in 1937, and Dzerzhinsky died in 1926.

questions.stem: In the Moscow show trials of 1936-1938, leading Old Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin:
options: admitted only to minor economic errors and were given short terms
confessed in public to invented crimes and were sentenced to death
were acquitted after foreign lawyers exposed the lack of real evidence
were tried in secret and released into exile in Western Europe
questions.explanation: Zinoviev and Kamenev were tried in August 1936 and Bukharin in March 1938. Each made public confessions to treason, sabotage and plotting with Trotsky, obtained by pressure and threats, and they were shot.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Great Terror of 1937-1938 shows that it reached far beyond the party elite?
options: arrests were made only after open jury trials held in each of the Soviet republics
NKVD 'mass operations' set regional quotas for arresting and shooting ordinary citizens
only members of the Politburo were arrested, while the rest of society was left untouched
it was confined to the army, and no civilians were arrested during these two years
questions.explanation: NKVD Order No. 00447 of July 1937 set quotas by region for former kulaks, criminals and other 'anti-Soviet elements', and national operations targeted groups such as Poles. Hundreds of thousands were shot and many more sent to the Gulag.

questions.stem: Why was the purge of the Red Army in 1937-1938 significant for the Soviet Union in 1941?
options: it gave the army control of the NKVD, so the military ran all the labour camps
it removed many experienced senior commanders, weakening the army just before the German invasion
it removed the political commissars, leaving the army without any party control by 1941
it doubled the size of the officer corps, creating too many generals to coordinate
questions.explanation: Marshal Tukhachevsky and many other senior officers were shot, and the officer corps lost much of its experience. This contributed to poor performance in the Winter War with Finland and the disasters of 1941.

questions.stem: The Gulag was:
options: the union of collective farms that managed rural output
the system of forced labour camps run by the secret police
the Soviet planning agency that set Five-Year Plan targets
the league of atheists that campaigned against the church
questions.explanation: The Main Camp Administration (Gulag) ran a vast network of labour camps whose prisoners built canals, railways and mines, such as the White Sea Canal. Gosplan was the planning agency.

questions.stem: Stalin justified forced collectivisation from 1929 mainly by the need to:
options: secure grain for the cities and for export to pay for industrialisation
return land to the nobles who had lost their estates in 1917
reduce the size of the industrial workforce in Moscow and the other major cities
end the state's control over the price of food in the market
questions.explanation: The grain procurement crisis of 1927-1928 convinced Stalin that peasants could not be relied on to sell enough grain. Collective farms made it easier for the state to take grain to feed workers and to export for machinery.

questions.stem: What was the aim of 'dekulakisation' announced by Stalin in December 1929?
options: to give the kulaks control of the new collective farms as their experienced managers
to lend the kulaks state money so they could buy tractors for their villages
to exempt the kulaks from collectivisation in return for paying higher taxes
to 'liquidate the kulaks as a class' by seizing their property and deporting them
questions.explanation: Peasants labelled kulaks, often loosely, had property seized and were shot, sent to camps or deported to remote regions. Removing them was meant to break village resistance and frighten others into joining collective farms.

questions.stem: In his article 'Dizzy with Success' (March 1930), Stalin blamed local officials for excesses. Which development best explains why he wrote it?
options: Collectivisation had been completed everywhere and no further work was needed
Western governments had imposed sanctions that blocked Soviet grain exports
The kulaks had been invited back to run the farms and needed reassurance
Peasant resistance, including killing livestock, threatened the spring sowing
questions.explanation: Forced collectivisation provoked riots and the mass slaughter of animals, and Stalin feared a collapse of the harvest. Many peasants left the collectives after the article, but the drive resumed later in 1930. Collectivisation was far from complete in March 1930.

questions.stem: Which was a major consequence of collectivisation in 1932-1933?
options: the return of private farming across the Soviet Union by 1934
a rapid rise in livestock numbers as farms shared their animals
a famine in which millions died, especially in Ukraine and Kazakhstan
a grain surplus so large that the state had to stop all exports for a year
questions.explanation: High procurement quotas, disruption and repression caused a famine that killed millions; in Ukraine it is called the Holodomor. Livestock numbers fell sharply, and the state continued to export grain during the famine.

questions.stem: The Soviet Five-Year Plans gave top priority to:
options: small private workshops and family-run businesses in towns
luxury goods for export to pay off the Tsarist foreign debt
heavy industry such as coal, steel, electricity and machinery
consumer goods such as clothing, furniture and household items
questions.explanation: Gosplan set high targets for heavy industry and new industrial centres such as Magnitogorsk. Consumer goods were neglected, so living standards for many workers fell in the early 1930s.

questions.stem: The Stakhanovite movement of the mid-1930s encouraged workers to:
options: go on strike for shorter hours, following a miner who led a large protest in the Donbas in 1935
leave the factories for the collective farms to help gather the harvest each autumn
join the army reserve and train in the evenings after their shifts in the factory
break production records, following a miner said to have cut 102 tonnes of coal in one shift
questions.explanation: In August 1935 Alexei Stakhanov was reported to have mined 102 tonnes of coal in under six hours, many times the norm, in a shift arranged for the purpose. Record-breakers received higher pay and privileges, and norms were raised for others. Strikes were not tolerated.

questions.stem: Historians judge the First Five-Year Plan (1928-1932) a qualified success. Which pair of points best supports this view?
options: Full achievement of every target, but a decline in the number of industrial workers
Rapid growth of private trade, but the closure of most state-owned factories
Large increases in coal, iron and steel output, but waste, poor quality and falling living standards
Large increases in consumer goods, but a fall in coal, steel and electricity output
questions.explanation: Heavy industrial output rose dramatically and new plants were built, although many inflated targets were missed. The costs were waste, shoddy goods, chaotic planning and hardship for workers and peasants. Consumer goods lagged and private trade was suppressed.

questions.stem: Socialist realism, made the official style for Soviet artists and writers in 1934, required works to:
options: explore the artist's private feelings without any political message
experiment with abstract forms that ordinary people found hard to read
criticise the party openly so that its mistakes could be corrected
show Soviet life optimistically and promote the building of socialism
questions.explanation: The First Congress of Soviet Writers in 1934 adopted socialist realism, which demanded art that was accessible, optimistic and politically useful, with heroic workers and party leaders. Experimental and abstract art of the 1920s was attacked as 'formalism'.

questions.stem: In January 1936 Pravda attacked Shostakovich's opera Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk. This shows that under Stalin:
options: artists were free to experiment as long as their work was popular with Western audiences
the Communist Party left judgments about culture to independent critics and audiences
even famous artists risked official condemnation if their work displeased the leadership
music was the only art form that escaped censorship because it had no words to check
questions.explanation: The unsigned article, reportedly after Stalin saw the opera, condemned it as chaotic and formalist, and the opera disappeared from Soviet stages. It showed that culture was subject to party control and that no artist was safe.

questions.stem: Which policy shows the Soviet state's attack on religion in the late 1920s and 1930s?
options: allowing churches to run all primary schools so long as they also taught Marxist ideas
banning only Islam while giving the Orthodox Church new land and freedom to preach
closing and demolishing churches and arresting clergy, supported by the League of the Militant Godless
making the Orthodox Church the official state religion in return for its support of the plans
questions.explanation: A 1929 law restricted religious activity to registered worship, and thousands of churches, mosques and synagogues were closed, with clergy arrested or shot. Moscow's Cathedral of Christ the Saviour was blown up in 1931. The campaign targeted all faiths.

questions.stem: The historian Nicholas Timasheff described changes in Soviet social policy in the mid-1930s as 'the Great Retreat'. Which policy best fits this description?
options: Abolishing all school examinations and letting students set their own curriculum
Allowing the return of private land ownership to peasants on the collective farms
Ending the cult of Stalin and restoring open debate inside the Communist Party
Banning most abortions and making divorce harder in 1936 to strengthen the family
questions.explanation: After the radicalism of the 1920s, the regime restored traditional values: the 1936 family law banned most abortions and made divorce costly, and schools returned to discipline, exams and uniforms. Collective farms stayed and the cult of Stalin grew stronger.

questions.stem: How did Stalin's industrialisation change the lives of many Soviet women in the 1930s?
options: women gained equal pay and full equality in senior party and state posts
millions entered paid work while still doing most housework, a 'double burden'
most women were sent home from work to raise children as the plans required
women were barred from joining the Communist Party and all of the trade unions
questions.explanation: The labour needs of the plans drew millions of women into factories, mines and offices, but they kept responsibility for children and housework. Few women reached senior posts, and pay was not equal in practice.

questions.stem: Under the Comintern's 'Third Period' line from 1928, foreign communist parties were told to:
options: form broad popular fronts with socialists and liberals against the fascist parties
dissolve themselves and join the largest socialist party in each country
support the League of Nations and its policy of collective security
treat social democrats as 'social fascists' and refuse to cooperate with them
questions.explanation: The Third Period line assumed capitalism was about to collapse, so moderate socialists were attacked as the main enemy. In Germany this split the left as the Nazis rose. Popular fronts replaced this line from 1935.

questions.stem: Which development marked the Soviet shift to a policy of 'collective security' in the mid-1930s?
options: signing a non-aggression pact with Germany in August 1934
joining the League of Nations in 1934 and signing a pact with France in 1935
signing the Anti-Comintern Pact with Germany and Japan in 1936
leaving the League of Nations in protest at its sanctions on Italy
questions.explanation: Alarmed by Hitler, Foreign Commissar Maxim Litvinov sought alliances with the Western democracies: the USSR joined the League in September 1934 and signed mutual assistance pacts with France and Czechoslovakia in 1935. The Anti-Comintern Pact was directed against the USSR.

questions.stem: Why did Stalin sign the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact in August 1939?
options: A promise from Hitler to hand over Germany's colonies in Africa to the Soviet Union
Distrust of Britain and France after Munich, a wish to gain time, and gains in Eastern Europe
Agreement with Nazi ideology and a plan for a permanent alliance against all communists
A British request that the USSR stay neutral so that Britain could fight Germany alone
questions.explanation: Excluded from the Munich Agreement and doubtful of Western commitment, Stalin chose a pact that kept the USSR out of war and gave it a secret sphere of influence in Poland, the Baltic states and Bessarabia. The pact was pragmatic; the regimes remained ideological enemies.

questions.stem: Under the secret protocol of the Nazi-Soviet Pact, the Soviet Union occupied:
options: Czechoslovakia in September 1939 and Hungary in 1940
eastern Poland in September 1939 and the Baltic states in 1940
the Rhineland in September 1939 and the whole of Austria in 1940
all of Finland in September 1939 and Norway in 1940
questions.explanation: Soviet forces invaded eastern Poland on 17 September 1939, and Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were annexed in 1940, as was Bessarabia from Romania. Finland resisted in the Winter War of 1939-1940 and kept its independence.

questions.stem: Which factor best shows ideology shaping Soviet foreign policy in 1928-1941?
options: The belief in world revolution led Stalin to invade Western Europe in the 1930s
The belief that religion should guide policy led to alliances with Catholic Spain
The belief that capitalist states would encircle and attack the USSR made security the first priority
The belief that all capitalist states were natural allies made Stalin trust Hitler completely in the spring of 1941
questions.explanation: Marxist-Leninist ideology taught that capitalist powers were hostile, which reinforced Stalin's focus on defending 'socialism in one country' and kept him suspicious of both fascist and democratic states. Socialism in One Country put the security of the USSR ahead of spreading revolution.

questions.stem: Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, Operation Barbarossa, took the Red Army by surprise largely because:
options: Britain had promised Stalin that it would invade France before Germany struck
Stalin had dismissed repeated warnings, believing Hitler would not attack so soon
the Soviet Union had broken off all its intelligence gathering after the 1939 pact
the Red Army had been sent to fight Japan in Manchuria in the spring of 1941
questions.explanation: Stalin received warnings from his own agents and from Britain but treated them as provocations, and kept supplying Germany under the 1940 trade agreement. The 1941 neutrality pact with Japan had in fact reduced the threat in the east.
